sections.title: section, article or div?
body: The most common question in semantic HTML has a short ruler.
**`<article>`** — it makes sense on its own, outside the page. A post, a news item, a comment, a product card. The test: could you publish this in an RSS feed?
**`<section>`** — a thematic block **inside** something larger, and one that has a heading. If you cannot give it a heading, it is probably not a `section`.
**`<div>`** — it means nothing, and that is fine. It is the element for grouping on purely visual grounds: a container that exists only to receive a `display: flex`.
`<div>` is not a defeat. Using `<section>` where all you needed was layout is worse: it creates false semantic structure, and the screen reader announces a region that does not exist.

pt.title: section, article ou div?
pt.body: ["A dúvida mais comum do HTML semântico tem uma régua curta.",["**`<article>`** — faz sentido sozinho, fora da página. Um post, uma notícia, um comentário, um cartão de produto. Teste: dá para publicar isto num feed RSS?","**`<section>`** — um bloco temático **dentro** de algo maior, e que tem um título. Se você não consegue dar um título a ele, provavelmente não é uma `section`.","**`<div>`** — não significa nada, e está certo assim. É o elemento para agrupar por motivo puramente visual: um contêiner que existe só para receber um `display: flex`."],"`<div>` não é derrota. Usar `<section>` onde só havia necessidade de layout é pior: cria estrutura semântica falsa, e o leitor de tela anuncia uma região que não existe."]

lessons.topic: Forms, fields, labels and native validation
lessons.title: Forms, fields, labels and native validation

pt.title: Formulários, campos, rótulos e validação nativa

es.title: Formularios, campos, etiquetas y validación nativa

fr.title: Formulaires, champs, libellés et validation native

it.title: Moduli, campi, etichette e validazione nativa

sections.title: A field with no label is a broken field
body: Every field needs a `<label>` tied to it. The tie is the `for` pointing at the `id`:

body.text:
<label for="email">E-mail</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" required />

body: The tie does three things at once: the screen reader announces the label when the field takes focus, clicking the text focuses the field, and the touch target on a phone grows — which matters more than it looks on checkboxes.
A `placeholder` does **not** replace a label. It disappears as soon as the person starts typing, and then nobody knows what that field was any more. It is a complement, not a substitute.

pt.title: Campo sem rótulo é campo quebrado
pt.body: ["Todo campo precisa de um `<label>` ligado a ele. A ligação é pelo `for` que aponta para o `id`:",{"code":"html","text":"<label for=\"email\">E-mail</label>\n<input type=\"email\" id=\"email\" name=\"email\" required />"},"A ligação faz três coisas de uma vez: o leitor de tela anuncia o rótulo quando o campo recebe foco, clicar no texto foca o campo, e a área de toque no celular cresce — o que importa mais do que parece em caixas de seleção.","`placeholder` **não** substitui rótulo. Ele some quando a pessoa começa a digitar, e aí ninguém mais sabe o que aquele campo era. É complemento, não substituto."]

sections.title: The field type changes the keyboard
body: On a computer, `type="email"` and `type="text"` look the same. On a phone they do not: the type picks which keyboard appears.
`email` — brings the `@` and the dot onto the first screen.
`tel` — the big numeric keypad, the dialling one.
`number` — numeric, but careful: it refuses leading zeros and formatting characters, so it does **not** work for postcodes, national IDs or card numbers.
`url`, `date`, `search` — each with its own keyboard and its own native picker.
For a postcode or a masked phone number, the pair that works is `type="text"` with `inputmode="numeric"`: a numeric keypad, without the restrictions of `number`.

pt.title: O tipo do campo muda o teclado
pt.body: ["No computador, `type=\"email\"` e `type=\"text\"` parecem iguais. No celular, não: o tipo escolhe qual teclado aparece.",["`email` — traz o `@` e o ponto na primeira tela.","`tel` — teclado numérico grande, o de discagem.","`number` — numérico, mas cuidado: ele recusa zeros à esquerda e caracteres de formatação, então **não** serve para CEP, CPF nem cartão.","`url`, `date`, `search` — cada um com o seu teclado e o seu seletor nativo."],"Para CEP e telefone com máscara, o par que funciona é `type=\"text\"` com `inputmode=\"numeric\"`: teclado numérico, sem as restrições de `number`."]

sections.title: Native validation, and where it stops
body: The browser validates on its own from attributes, with no line of JavaScript:

body.text:
<input type="email" required />
<input type="text" minlength="3" maxlength="40" />
<input type="text" pattern="[0-9]{5}-[0-9]{3}" />

body: And you can style the state with `:valid`, `:invalid` and — most useful of all — `:user-invalid`, which only turns red **after** the person has interacted with the field. Without it, a form is born entirely red before anyone types anything.

**Validation in the browser is convenience, never security.** Anybody removes a `required` through the inspector in two seconds. The server validates everything again, always — the client-side one exists to avoid the trip to the server, not to protect it.

pt.title: Validação nativa, e onde ela para
pt.body: ["O navegador valida sozinho com atributos, sem uma linha de JavaScript:",{"code":"html","text":"<input type=\"email\" required />\n<input type=\"text\" minlength=\"3\" maxlength=\"40\" />\n<input type=\"text\" pattern=\"[0-9]{5}-[0-9]{3}\" />"},"E dá para estilizar o estado com `:valid`, `:invalid` e — o mais útil — `:user-invalid`, que só pinta de vermelho **depois** de a pessoa ter interagido com o campo. Sem ele, um formulário nasce todo vermelho antes de alguém digitar nada.","**Validação no navegador é conveniência, nunca segurança.** Qualquer pessoa remove um `required` pelo inspetor em dois segundos. O servidor valida tudo de novo, sempre — a do cliente existe para evitar a viagem até o servidor, não para proteger dele."]

lessons.topic: Tables, responsive images and media
lessons.title: Tables, responsive images and media

pt.title: Tabelas, imagens responsivas e mídia

es.title: Tablas, imágenes responsivas y multimedia

fr.title: Tableaux, images responsives et médias

it.title: Tabelle, immagini responsive e contenuti multimediali

sections.title: A table is for data, not for layout
body: A table exists for tabular data — something with rows, columns and meaning in both. A well-marked table tells the screen reader which column each cell belongs to, and the person can navigate between them:

body.text:
Marks for the term
StudentMark
Ana9.0

body: `scope` is what makes the difference: without it, the screen reader reads "9.0" without saying whose or of what. With it, it reads "Ana, Mark, 9.0".
Using a table to position things on screen was normal in the 1990s and today is a mistake: it creates false data structure, and Flexbox and Grid do it better. Layout is the next half of the course.

pt.title: Tabela é para dado, não para layout
pt.body:
["Tabela existe para dado tabular — coisa que tem linha, coluna e sentido em ambas. Uma tabela bem marcada diz ao leitor de tela a que coluna cada célula pertence, e a pessoa consegue navegar entre elas:",{"code":"html","text":"
Notas do semestre
AlunoNota
Ana9,0
"},"O `scope` é o que faz a diferença: sem ele, o leitor de tela lê "9,0" sem dizer de quem nem de quê. Com ele, lê "Ana, Nota, 9,0".","Usar tabela para posicionar coisas na tela foi normal nos anos 90 e hoje é erro: cria estrutura de dados falsa, e Flexbox e Grid resolvem melhor. Layout é a próxima metade do curso."]

sections.title: Images that do not waste bandwidth
body: Serving the same 2000px image to a phone throws away the bandwidth and the battery of whoever has least of both. `srcset` lets the browser choose:

`width` and `height` do not fix the size when there is CSS — they state the **aspect ratio**, and that is what stops the page from jumping when the image finishes loading. `loading="lazy"` defers whatever is off screen.

body.alt: Three rectangles of different sizes labelled 400w, 800w and 1600w, under the labels phone, tablet and desktop
body.caption: `srcset` offers all three; the one who chooses is the browser, which knows the screen width and its density — things the server does not know.

body: `alt` describes the image for whoever cannot see it. A purely decorative image takes `alt=""` — empty, not absent: that way the screen reader ignores it instead of announcing the file name.

pt.title: Imagens que não desperdiçam banda
pt.body: ["Servir a mesma imagem de 2000px para um celular é jogar fora banda e bateria de quem tem menos dos dois. `srcset` deixa o navegador escolher:",{"code":"html","text":""},"`width` e `height` não fixam o tamanho quando há CSS — eles informam a **proporção**, e é isso que impede a página de pular quando a imagem termina de carregar. `loading="lazy"` adia o que está fora da tela.",{"image":"data:image/svg+xml,400w800w1600wcelulartabletdesktopo%20navegadorescolhe%20uma,n%C3%A3o%20as%20tr%C3%AAs","alt":"Três retângulos de tamanhos diferentes rotulados 400w, 800w e 1600w, sob os rótulos celular, tablet e desktop","caption":"O `srcset` oferece as três; quem escolhe é o navegador, que sabe a largura da tela e a densidade dela — coisas que o servidor não sabe."},"O `alt` descreve a imagem para quem não a vê. Imagem puramente decorativa leva `alt=""` — vazio, não ausente: assim o leitor de tela a ignora em vez de anunciar o nome do arquivo."]

sections.title: Video and audio
body: The native elements need no library for the common case:

body.text:
<video controls preload="metadata" poster="cover.jpg" width="640">
  <source src="lesson.webm" type="video/webm" />
  <source src="lesson.mp4" type="video/mp4" />
  <track kind="captions" src="lesson.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default />
</video>

body: Several `<source>` elements let the browser take the format it can play. `preload="metadata"` downloads only enough to know the duration — `auto` would download the whole video for someone who may never watch it.

The caption track is not optional in practice: it serves whoever cannot hear, whoever is somewhere noisy and whoever would rather read. And unlike the rest, it cannot be added later without producing the content again.

pt.title: Vídeo e áudio
pt.body:
["Os elementos nativos dispensam biblioteca para o caso comum:",{"code":"html","text":"<video controls preload="metadata" poster="capa.jpg" width="640">
  <source src="aula.webm" type="video/webm" />
  <source src="aula.mp4" type="video/mp4" />
  <track kind="captions" src="aula.vtt" srclang="pt" label="Português" default />
</video>"},"Vários `<source>` deixam o navegador pegar o formato que ele reproduz. `preload="metadata"` baixa só o suficiente para saber a duração — `auto` baixaria o vídeo inteiro de quem talvez não o assista.","A faixa de legenda não é opcional na prática: ela serve a quem não ouve, a quem está em lugar barulhento e a quem prefere ler. E, ao contrário do resto, ela não se acrescenta depois sem voltar a produzir o conteúdo."]

lessons.topic: Selectors, cascade, inheritance and specificity
lessons.title: Selectors, cascade, inheritance and specificity

pt.title: Seletores, cascata, herança e especificidade

es.title: Selectores, cascada, herencia y especificidad

fr.title: Sélecteurs, cascade, héritage et spécificité

it.title: Selettori, cascata, ereditarietà e specificità

sections.title: The vocabulary of selectors
body: A selector is the question "which elements?". The forms that solve almost everything:

body.text:
.card            { }   /* class */
#top             { }   /* id */
nav a            { }   /* descendant: every `a` inside nav */
nav > a          { }   /* direct child */
li + li          { }   /* immediately following sibling */
a[href^="http"]  { }   /* attribute starting with */
li:nth-child(2n) { }   /* pseudo-class */

body: In practice, **a class solves 90% of cases**, and it is what you should prefer. An id is unique per page and, as the next section shows, carries a weight in specificity that gets in the way more than it helps.

pt.title: O vocabulário dos seletores
pt.body:
["Seletor é a pergunta "quais elementos?". As formas que resolvem quase tudo:",{"code":"css","text":".cartao          { }   /* classe */
#topo            { }   /* id */
nav a            { }   /* descendente: todo `a` dentro de nav */
nav > a          { }   /* filho direto */
li + li          { }   /* irmão imediatamente seguinte */
a[href^="http"]  { }   /* atributo que começa com */
li:nth-child(2n) { }   /* pseudo-classe */"},"Na prática, **classe resolve 90% dos casos**, e é o que se deve preferir. Id é único por página e, como se vê na próxima seção, tem um peso na especificidade que atrapalha mais do que ajuda."]

sections.title: Specificity: the sum that decides who wins
body: When two rules reach the same element and declare the same property, the more specific one wins. Specificity is a trio of numbers — **(ids, classes, elements)** — compared from left to right:

body.text:
p                 /* (0,0,1) */
.warning          /* (0,1,0)  beats p */
nav a.active      /* (0,1,2) */
#top              /* (1,0,0)  beats everything above */

body: The first number crushes the others: **one id beats any number of classes**. That is why styling by id ends up forcing the next person to use `!important` — and once `!important` gets into a file, it spreads.
A specificity tie is broken by order: the last rule written wins.

pt.title: Especificidade: a conta que decide quem ganha
pt.body:
["Quando duas regras atingem o mesmo elemento e declaram a mesma propriedade, vence a mais específica. A especificidade é um trio de números — **(ids, classes, elementos)** — comparado da esquerda para a direita:",{"code":"css","text":"p                 /* (0,0,1) */
.aviso            /* (0,1,0)  vence de p */
nav a.ativo       /* (0,1,2) */
#topo             /* (1,0,0)  vence de tudo acima */"},"O primeiro número esmaga os outros: **um id vence qualquer quantidade de classes**. É por isso que estilizar por id acaba forçando o próximo a usar `!important` — e uma vez que `!important` entra num arquivo, ele se espalha.","Empate de especificidade é desempatado pela ordem: a última regra escrita ganha."]

sections.title: Cascade and inheritance are different things
body: **Cascade** is how the browser chooses between rules competing for the same element: origin, `!important`, specificity and, finally, order.
**Inheritance** is something else: some properties pass from parent to child without anyone asking. `color`, `font-family` and `line-height` inherit; `border`, `padding` and `background` do not.

The distinction matters because it explains a common mistake: setting `font-family` on the `body` works for the whole page (inheritance), but setting `border` on the `body` draws no border on any child. And there is the hybrid case of `<button>`, which does **not** inherit the font by default — hence the `font: inherit` line that shows up in almost every serious stylesheet.

pt.title: Cascata e herança são coisas diferentes
pt.body: ["**Cascata** é como o navegador escolhe entre regras que disputam o mesmo elemento: origem, `!important`, especificidade e, por fim, ordem.","**Herança** é outra coisa: algumas propriedades passam de pai para filho sem ninguém pedir. `color`, `font-family` e `line-height` herdam; `border`, `padding` e `background` não.","A distinção importa porque explica um erro comum: definir `font-family` no `body` funciona para a página inteira (herança), mas definir `border` no `body` não desenha borda nenhuma nos filhos. E há o caso híbrido do `<button>`, que **não** herda a fonte por padrão — daí a linha `font: inherit` que aparece em quase todo CSS sério."]

lessons.topic: Box model, box-sizing and units (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)
lessons.title: Box model, box-sizing and units (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)

pt.title: Modelo de caixa, box-sizing e unidades (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)

es.title: Modelo de caja, box-sizing y unidades (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)

fr.title: Modèle de boîte, box-sizing et unités (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)

it.title: Modello a scatola, box-sizing e unità (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)

sections.title: Everything is a box
body: Every element is a rectangle with four layers, from the inside out: **content**, **padding**, **border** and **margin**.
Padding is inner space — it pushes the content away from the border and takes the background colour. Margin is outer space — it separates this box from its neighbours and is transparent.

One detail confuses everybody once: **adjacent vertical margins merge**. Two paragraphs with 20px of margin below and above do not end up 40px apart; they end up 20 apart. That is *margin collapsing*, it only applies vertically, and it is the reason many people use flex/grid `gap` instead of margin.

pt.title: Toda coisa é uma caixa
pt.body: ["Cada elemento é um retângulo com quatro camadas, de dentro para fora: **conteúdo**, **padding**, **borda** e **margem**.","Padding é espaço interno — ele empurra o conteúdo para longe da borda e recebe a cor de fundo. Margem é espaço externo — separa esta caixa das vizinhas e é transparente.","Um detalhe que confunde todo mundo uma vez: **margens verticais adjacentes se fundem**. Dois parágrafos com 20px de margem embaixo e em cima não ficam com 40px de distância; ficam com 20. É o *colapso de margens*, vale só na vertical, e é a razão de muita gente usar `gap` do flex/grid em vez de margem."]

sections.title: box-sizing, and the first line of every stylesheet
body: By default, `width` measures only the content. So a box declared at 200px plus padding and border occupies **more** than 200px:
That turns any layout into mental arithmetic. The fix is one line, and it opens practically every modern stylesheet:
With `border-box`, `width: 200px` means 200px on screen, with the padding and border **inside**. It is the behaviour everybody expected from the start.

pt.title: box-sizing, e a primeira linha de todo CSS

sections.title: Which unit for what
body: Each unit answers a different question, and choosing the wrong one is the source of half the accessibility problems in typography.
**`px`** — absolute. Good for borders and shadows, where the value really is physical.

**`rem`** — a multiple of the root font size. It is the default for typography and spacing, because it **respects whoever enlarged the font in the browser**. Text sized in `px` ignores that preference.
**`em`** — a multiple of the element's own font size. Useful for spacing that should follow the text, but careful: it compounds in nested elements.
**`%`** — relative to the container. Width.
**`vw` / `vh`** — relative to the window. Good for full screens; on a phone, prefer `svh`/`dvh`, which cope with the browser bar appearing and disappearing.
The practical rule that settles almost everything: **`rem` for text and space, `%` or `fr` for width, `px` only for fine detail.**

pt.title: Qual unidade para quê
pt.body: ["Cada unidade responde a uma pergunta diferente, e escolher errado é a origem de metade dos problemas de acessibilidade em tipografia.",["**`px`** — absoluto. Bom para borda e para sombra, onde o valor é físico mesmo.","**`rem`** — múltiplo da fonte-raiz. É o padrão para tipografia e espaçamento, porque **respeita quem aumentou a fonte no navegador**. Tamanho de texto em `px` ignora essa preferência.","**`em`** — múltiplo da fonte do próprio elemento. Útil para espaçamento que deve acompanhar o texto, mas cuidado: ele acumula em elementos aninhados.","**`%`** — relativo ao contêiner. Largura.","**`vw` / `vh`** — relativo à janela. Bom para telas cheias; no celular, prefira `svh`/`dvh`, que lidam com a barra do navegador que aparece e some."],"A regra prática que resolve quase tudo: **`rem` para texto e espaço, `%` ou `fr` para largura, `px` só para detalhes finos.**"]

lessons.topic: Positioning: static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky
lessons.title: Positioning: static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky

pt.title: Posicionamento: static, relative, absolute, fixed e sticky

es.title: Posicionamiento: static, relative, absolute, fixed y sticky

fr.title: Positionnement : static, relative, absolute, fixed et sticky

it.title: Posizionamento: static, relative, absolute, fixed e sticky

sections.title: The normal flow, and leaving it a little
body: By default every element is `position: static`: it stays where the flow put it, and `top`/`left` do nothing.

`position: relative` keeps the element in the flow — **its space stays reserved** — and shifts only the drawing. That is why it is almost never used to move things: it is used to become the **anchor** of an `absolute` child, which is the next section's subject.

pt.title: O fluxo normal, e sair um pouco dele
pt.body: ["Por padrão todo elemento é `position: static`: ele fica onde o fluxo o colocou, e `top`/`left` não fazem nada.","`position: relative` mantém o elemento no fluxo — **o espaço dele continua reservado** — e desloca só o desenho. Por isso ele quase nunca é usado para mover coisas: é usado para virar **âncora** de um filho `absolute`, que é o assunto da próxima seção."]

sections.title: absolute and the positioning context
body: `position: absolute` takes the element out of the flow: its space stops existing and the neighbours close up as if it were not there. It positions itself relative to the **nearest positioned ancestor** — any one that is not `static`.

It is the most used pattern in all of CSS: the parent becomes `relative` purely to serve as a reference, and the child hangs off its corner. **Forgetting the `relative` on the parent** is the classic defect — the badge climbs to the corner of the page, because with no positioned ancestor the reference becomes the window.

pt.title: absolute e o contexto de posicionamento

sections.title: fixed and sticky
body: `fixed` pins the element to the window: it does not move when the page scrolls. It is what holds this portal's top bar in place.
`sticky` is the hybrid: the element scrolls normally until it reaches the declared limit, and sticks there.

Two gotchas with `sticky` explain almost every "it does not work" case: it **requires** a declared offset (`top`, `bottom`…), without which it does nothing; and it sticks inside its **parent**, not the window — if the parent has `overflow: hidden` or ends soon, the effect ends with it.

pt.title: fixed e sticky

lessons.topic: Flexbox: axes, alignment and distribution
lessons.title: Flexbox: axes, alignment and distribution

pt.title: Flexbox: eixos, alinhamento e distribuição

es.title: Flexbox: ejes, alineación y distribución

fr.title: Flexbox : axes, alignement et distribution

it.title: Flexbox: assi, allineamento e distribuzione

sections.title: Everything depends on the main axis
body: Flexbox arranges the children along **one** axis. `flex-direction` picks which:

Understanding that settles the confusion that slows learners down most: `justify-content` acts on the **main axis** and `align-items` on the **cross** one. Since the default is `row`, `justify-content` looks "horizontal" and `align-items` looks "vertical" — until somebody writes `flex-direction: column`, and the two swap meaning.
The right question is never "how do I centre horizontally?", it is "what is my main axis?".

body.caption: Swapping `row` for `column` does not just move the items: it **swaps** the two alignment properties around. That is why the one that used to work "stopped working".

pt.title: Tudo depende do eixo principal

sections.title: Aligning and distributing
body: Centring in both directions, once a puzzle, is three lines today. Rather than showing the three on their own, it is worth reading a whole navigation bar — which is where these properties really turn up — with the explanation of each piece beside it:

parts.note: From here on the direct children of `.bar` are flex items. Nothing happens to the grandchildren — flex applies one level only.

Aligns on the **cross** axis. With `flex-direction: row` (the default), the cross axis is the vertical one: this is what puts the logo and the links at the same height even though they are different sizes.
The space between the items. `gap` leaves nothing over at the ends, does not collapse, and does away with the `:last-child { margin: 0 }` every old stylesheet carries.
The bar's inner space. Note that it is NOT `gap`: one is the frame, the other is the distance between the items.

The most useful trick in flexbox. `margin: auto` eats all the free space on that side, so this item — and everything after it — is pushed to the right. It does what `justify-content: space-between` would do, but for ONE item, and without touching the rest.

The most mysterious and most useful line. A flex item does not shrink below its own content by default, and a long title bursts the bar instead of getting an ellipsis. `min-width: 0` gives the permission to shrink back.

body: On the main axis, the values you use are `flex-start`, `center`, `flex-end`, `space-between` (the ends flush against the edges, equal space between the items) and `space-evenly` (equal space everywhere, edges included).

pt.title: Alinhar e distribuir

sections.title: Growing, shrinking and the basis
body: The `flex` property is a shorthand for three things: how much the item may grow, how much it may shrink, and what size it starts from.

body.text:
.side   { flex: 0 0 240px; }  /* does not grow, does not shrink: a fixed 240px */
.middle { flex: 1 1 auto; }   /* takes whatever is left */
.equal  { flex: 1; }          /* shorthand for 1 1 0: all the same width */

body: The difference between `flex: 1` and `flex: 1 1 auto` trips a lot of people up: with a basis of `0`, the items all end up the same size; with a basis of `auto`, each one's content matters, and an item with a long text ends up larger than the others.

And a flex item **does not shrink below its content** by default, which makes a long text burst the container. The cure is `min-width: 0` on the item — the most mysterious and most useful line in flexbox.

pt.title: Crescer, encolher e a base
pt.body: ["A propriedade `flex` é um atalho para três coisas: quanto o item pode crescer, quanto pode encolher e de que tamanho ele parte.",{"code":"css","text":".lado    { flex: 0 0 240px; }  /* não cresce, não encolhe: 240px fixos */\n.miolo   { flex: 1 1 auto; }   /* ocupa o que sobrar */\n.igual   { flex: 1; }          /* atalho de 1 1 0: todos com a mesma largura */"},"A diferença entre `flex: 1` e `flex: 1 1 auto` derruba muita gente: com base `0`, os itens ficam todos do mesmo tamanho; com base `auto`, o conteúdo de cada um influencia, e um item com texto longo fica maior que os outros.","E um item flex **não encolhe abaixo do conteúdo** por padrão, o que faz texto longo estourar o contêiner. A cura é `min-width: 0` no item — a linha mais misteriosa e mais útil do flexbox."]

lessons.topic: CSS Grid: rows, columns, areas and the implicit grid
lessons.title: CSS Grid: rows, columns, areas and the implicit grid

pt.title: CSS Grid: linhas, colunas, áreas e grid implícito

es.title: CSS Grid: filas, columnas, áreas y grilla implícita

fr.title: CSS Grid : lignes, colonnes, zones et grille implicite

it.title: CSS Grid: righe, colonne, aree e griglia implicita

sections.title: Two dimensions at once
body: Flexbox arranges along one axis; Grid arranges rows and columns at the same time. The new unit is `fr`, a fraction of the free space:

That is a fixed sidebar and a content area taking the rest — exactly this portal's skeleton. It could be done in flexbox, but it would require declaring the behaviour on each child; in grid, the parent declares the shape and the children need to know nothing.

pt.title: Duas dimensões de uma vez

sections.title: Named areas: the layout drawn out
body: The most readable form of grid is to name the regions and draw them:
The CSS starts to **look like** the layout, and rearranging everything for a phone means rewriting the three quoted lines inside a media query — without touching a single child.

pt.title: Áreas nomeadas: o layout desenhado

sections.title: The implicit grid and grids that adjust themselves
body: If you declare two columns and six items arrive, the grid creates new rows on its own: that is the **implicit grid**, controlled by `grid-auto-rows`.
The most profitable combination in modern CSS makes a responsive grid **with no media query at all**:
It reads: as many columns as fit, each at least 220px and sharing the rest equally. The grid rearranges itself at any width.
`auto-fill` keeps the empty columns reserved; `auto-fit` collapses them, making the existing items stretch to fill. With few items on a wide screen, the choice between the two is very visible.

pt.title: Grid implícito e grades que se ajustam

lessons.topic: CSS variables and organising stylesheets
lessons.title: CSS variables and organising stylesheets

pt.title: Variáveis CSS e organização de estilos

es.title: Variables CSS y organización de estilos

fr.title: Variables CSS et organisation des styles

it.title: Variabili CSS e organizzazione degli stili

sections.title: Custom properties
body: CSS variables are declared with two hyphens and read with `var()`:

The difference from a preprocessor's variables is decisive: these **exist in the browser**. They inherit, they can be swapped inside a selector, they respond to a media query and they are readable and writable from JavaScript at run time. A Sass variable disappears at compile time; this one is still there.

pt.title: Custom properties

sections.title: Light and dark themes with one switch
body: Because variables inherit, swapping a whole theme is redeclaring them in a scope above:

The rest of the stylesheet never mentions a theme colour: it reads `var(--background)` and does not know two exist. Swapping the theme becomes adding an attribute on `<html>` — one line of JavaScript, without rewriting a single rule. It is exactly how the portal and the vitrine do it.

pt.title: Tema claro e escuro com uma chave

sections.title: Organising without turning it into archaeology
body: A stylesheet that grows without order becomes a file nobody dares delete anything from. Three habits hold that back:
**A predictable order in the file**: reset, variables, base, components, utilities, media queries. A new rule has an obvious place to go.
**Low, flat specificity**: a simple class, with almost no nesting. A four-level selector forces the next one to have five.
**Name it for what the thing is, not for what it looks like**: `.warning` survives the decision to make the warning blue; `.red-text` does not.
If an `!important` has shown up, the cause was almost always an over-specific selector further back. The fix is to lower that one's specificity, not to raise this one's.

pt.title: Organizar sem virar arqueologia
pt.body: ["Um CSS que cresce sem ordem vira um arquivo em que ninguém ousa apagar nada. Três hábitos seguram isso:",["**Ordem previsível no arquivo**: reset, variáveis, base, componentes, utilitários, media queries. Regra nova tem um lugar óbvio para entrar.","**Especificidade baixa e plana**: classe simples, quase sem aninhar. Seletor com quatro níveis obriga o próximo a ter cinco.","**Nome pelo que a coisa é, não pelo que ela parece**: `.aviso` sobrevive à decisão de deixar o aviso azul; `.texto-vermelho` não."],"Se um `!important` apareceu, quase sempre a causa foi um seletor específico demais lá atrás. O conserto é baixar a especificidade daquele, não subir a deste."]

lessons.topic: Responsiveness: mobile first, media queries and container queries
lessons.title: Responsiveness: mobile first, media queries and container queries

pt.title: Responsividade: mobile first, media queries e container queries

es.title: Responsividad: mobile first, media queries y container queries

fr.title: Responsive : mobile first, media queries et container queries

it.title: Responsive: mobile first, media query e container query

sections.title: Mobile first is about what the default is
body: Mobile first is not "start by designing the phone": it is **writing the phone's CSS with no media query at all**, and using media queries only to add what larger screens allow.

The order matters more than it looks. Written the other way round — desktop first, with `max-width` — the phone has to **undo** rules, and undoing costs more lines and more specificity than adding. On top of that, the weakest device ends up downloading and applying the CSS it will not use.

pt.title: Mobile first é sobre o que é padrão

sections.title: Media queries beyond width
body: Width is the most used, and far from the only one:

The `prefers-reduced-motion` one is the most forgotten and the one that matters most to whoever needs it: there are people for whom a sliding animation causes real nausea. Respecting it means switching transitions off inside that query.
`hover: none` solves the menu that "does not open on the phone": effects hung off `:hover` do not exist on touch.

pt.title: Media queries além da largura

sections.title: Container queries: the component that measures itself
body: A media query asks the size of the **window**. That breaks down for reusable components: the same card may be in a narrow bar or filling the whole screen, and the window cannot tell the two cases apart.
Container queries ask the size of the **container**:
The card starts adapting to the space **it** was given, not to the size of the monitor. It is the right answer for a component library, and today it is supported in every current browser.

pt.title: Container queries: o componente que se mede

lessons.topic: Transitions, animations and transforms
lessons.title: Transitions, animations and transforms

pt.title: Transições, animações e transformações

es.title: Transiciones, animaciones y transformaciones

fr.title: Transitions, animations et transformations

it.title: Transizioni, animazioni e trasformazioni

sections.title: Transition: smoothing a change
body: `transition` interpolates between two values when the property changes:
The transition is declared on the **normal** state, not on the `:hover` — that way it applies on the way in and on the way out. Declared only on the `:hover`, the effect eases in and snaps out.
Avoid `transition: all`. It starts animating properties you did not know had changed, and it is a silent source of jank.

pt.title: Transição: suavizar uma mudança

sections.title: Transforms
body: `transform` moves, rotates, scales and skews without taking the element out of the flow: **its space stays reserved** where it always was, and nothing around it moves.
The order of the functions matters: rotating and then translating is not the same as translating and then rotating, because each one operates in the coordinate system the previous one left behind.

pt.title: Transformações

sections.title: Animations, and what each property costs
body: For something that happens on its own, `@keyframes` describes the path:

Note what is being animated, and it is the most profitable rule in this whole lesson: **animate `transform` and `opacity`.** They touch only composition, which the graphics card does on its own. Animating `width`, `top` or `margin` redoes the layout of everything around it on every frame, and that is what stutters on a phone.
And respect whoever asked for less motion:

pt.title: Animações, e o custo de cada propriedade

lessons.topic: Tailwind CSS: utilities, configuration and components
lessons.title: Tailwind CSS: utilities, configuration and components

pt.title: Tailwind CSS: utilitários, configuração e componentes

es.title: Tailwind CSS: utilidades, configuración y componentes

fr.title: Tailwind CSS : utilitaires, configuration et composants

it.title: Tailwind CSS: utility, configurazione e componenti

sections.title: The idea: one class, one property
body: Tailwind inverts how CSS is organised. Instead of naming components and describing them in a separate file, you compose the style in the HTML itself with classes of one property each:

body.text:
<button class="px-4 py-2 rounded bg-blue-500 text-white hover:bg-blue-600">
  Send
</button>

body: The real gain is not typing less — it is that **the CSS stops growing**. There is no name to invent, no file to hunt down, and deleting the HTML deletes the style with it. The orphan class nobody dares remove disappears.
The cost is equally real: the HTML gets cluttered, and reading a long stretch of it gets harder. It is a trade, not a victory.

pt.title: A ideia: uma classe, uma propriedade
pt.body: ["Tailwind inverte a organização do CSS. Em vez de nomear componentes e descrevê-los num arquivo à parte, você compõe o estilo no próprio HTML com classes de uma propriedade cada:",{"code":"html","text":"<button class=\"px-4 py-2 rounded bg-blue-500 text-white hover:bg-blue-600\">\n  Enviar\n</button>"},"O ganho real não é digitar menos — é que **o CSS para de crescer**. Não há nome a inventar, não há arquivo a caçar, e apagar o HTML apaga o estilo junto. Some a classe órfã que ninguém tem coragem de remover.","O custo é igualmente real: o HTML fica poluído, e a leitura de um trecho longo piora. É uma troca, não uma vitória."]

sections.title: Configuration is where the design system lives
body: The classes come out of a configurable scale. Customising the scale is what stops Tailwind from being a pile of magic values:

Once that is done, `bg-brand` is the brand colour everywhere, and changing it means editing one line. It is the same role the CSS variables of lesson 09 play — the difference is that here the scale also generates the classes.

pt.title: Configuração é onde o design system mora

sections.title: When not to use it
body: Repeating the same sequence of ten classes in fifteen places is a sign there was a component there. The right way out is the component of whatever framework you already use — a `<Button>` in React, a partial in the template — not a new class regrouping utilities.

And Tailwind does **not** excuse you from knowing CSS. Every class is a property: whoever does not understand specificity, the box model and flexbox does not understand `flex-1`, `min-w-0` or why the shadow disappeared. The twelve previous lessons are still the prerequisite.

The honest ruler: Tailwind pays off in a product with many components and a team sharing the scale. On a five-screen company site, hand-written CSS is smaller, more readable and brings no tooling along with it.

pt.title: Quando não usar
pt.body: ["Repetir a mesma sequência de dez classes em quinze lugares é sinal de que ali havia um componente. A saída certa é o componente do framework que você já usa — um `<Botao>` em React, um parcial no template —, não uma classe nova que reagrupa utilitários.","E Tailwind **não** dispensa saber CSS. Cada classe é uma propriedade: quem não entende especificidade, modelo de caixa e flexbox não entende `flex-1`, `min-w-0` nem por que a sombra sumiu. As doze aulas anteriores continuam sendo o pré-requisito.","A régua honesta: Tailwind rende em produto com muitos componentes e um time que compartilha a escala. Numa página institucional de cinco telas, o CSS escrito à mão é menor, mais legível e não traz ferramenta nenhuma junto."]

exercises.topic: Client, server and host: who asks and who answers
exercises.prompt: A web server needs to query a database in order to build its response. At that instant, what is it?
exercises.socraticHint: The roles describe the moment of the conversation, not the equipment. Who starts the conversation with the database?

choices.text: The database's client, because it is the one starting that request — and it is still a server in the conversation with the browser.
choices.why: The roles belong to the moment: the same machine can be a server in one conversation and a client in another, at the same time.

choices.text: It stays purely a server, because a machine configured as a server cannot take on another role.
choices.why: The configuration decides which programs it runs, not which role it holds in each conversation.

choices.text: It becomes an intermediate host, a category distinct from client and server.
choices.why: `Host` is the neutral term for any machine with an address, not a third role in the conversation.

choices.text: Neither, because the query happens inside the same local network and the roles do not apply.
choices.why: Distance changes nothing: whoever asks is the client, whether the other side is in the next rack or on another continent.

exercises.topic: Client, server and host: who asks and who answers
exercises.prompt: Match each term to what it describes. There are options left over in the right-hand column.
exercises.socraticHint: Two of these terms describe a role in a conversation; one describes the machine, regardless of what it is doing.

pairs.right: The one who starts the conversation and makes the request
The one who waits to be asked and returns the answer
Any machine with an address on the network
The number saying which program the data is meant for

rightDistractors: The physical cable joining two neighbouring machines
The program that translates domain names into addresses

exercises.topic: Packet, frame and socket
exercises.prompt: During a transfer, the frame's destination MAC address changes several times, while the packet's destination IP address stays the same. Why?
exercises.socraticHint: One of the two addresses points at the end of the journey; the other points at its next leg.

choices.text: The MAC addresses the next hop and is rewritten at every leg; the IP addresses the final destination and crosses the whole journey.
choices.why: It is the difference between the address on the envelope and the plate of the truck carrying it right now.

choices.text: The MAC changes because it is drawn at random for each transmission, to make tracking on the local network harder.
choices.why: The MAC is burned into the card. Some systems change it for privacy, but that is optional and does not happen per frame.

choices.text: The IP stays because it is encrypted by TLS and cannot be rewritten by the routers.
choices.why: TLS encrypts the content, not the IP header — which has to stay readable precisely so the packet can be routed.

choices.text: Both are rewritten, but the IP goes back to its original value before reaching the destination.
choices.why: The destination IP is not rewritten on the ordinary path; what does something similar is NAT, and only with the source address.

exercises.topic: Packet, frame and socket
exercises.prompt: Match each port to the service that usually listens on it. There are options left over in the right-hand column.
exercises.socraticHint: Two of them differ by one letter in the protocol name and by a layer of encryption.

pairs.right: HTTP
HTTPS
SSH
PostgreSQL

rightDistractors: DNS
SMTP

exercises.topic: Bandwidth, latency and throughput
exercises.prompt: A team complains that the video call with an office in Europe stutters. The provider offers to double the bandwidth. What should they expect?
exercises.socraticHint: Which of the three measures best explains a call that stutters? And which of them does a thicker pipe actually change?

choices.text: Little or no improvement, because the likely problem is latency — and that depends on distance, not on the bandwidth bought.
choices.why: A thicker pipe does not shorten the road: 150 ms stays 150 ms on any plan.

choices.text: A proportional improvement: twice the bandwidth halves the travel time.
choices.why: Bandwidth and travel time are independent quantities; doubling one does not change the other.

choices.text: A guaranteed improvement, because throughput always reaches the bandwidth that was bought.
choices.why: Throughput usually sits below the bandwidth — it is precisely the gap between the two that reveals the problem.

choices.text: It will get worse, because more bandwidth increases congestion along the path.
choices.why: More capacity does not create congestion; it simply does not solve what is not a capacity problem.

exercises.topic: Bandwidth, latency and throughput
exercises.prompt: A file of `T` bits is transferred over a path with throughput `v` bits per second, and the connection takes `L` seconds to establish before the first bit leaves. Write the expression for the total time, in seconds.
exercises.socraticHint: There are two terms that add up: one does not depend on the size of the file and the other does. Which is which?

exercises.topic: IP address, MAC address and ARP
exercises.prompt: Tick every true statement about IP and MAC addresses.
exercises.socraticHint: One of the two describes where the machine is; the other, which machine it is. Take the laptop to another network and see which of the two changes.

choices.text: The IP changes when the machine connects to another network.
choices.why: The IP describes a position, like a postal address.

choices.text: The MAC travels with the equipment wherever it goes.
choices.why: The MAC is the card's identity, burned into it.

choices.text: Ranges like `192.168.x.x` are reused inside every local network and do not exist on the internet.
choices.why: They are private ranges; the router translates to the public IP through NAT.

choices.text: A website's server sees the MAC address of the laptop that visited it.
choices.why: A MAC only means anything on the local link: the server sees the MAC of the last router on its own path.

choices.text: IPv6 exists to give more speed than IPv4.
choices.why: It exists because IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses ran out — it is a question of space, not of speed.

exercises.topic: IP address, MAC address and ARP
exercises.prompt: On a public network, a machine answers ARP questions posing as the router and starts receiving its neighbours' traffic. What makes this attack possible?
exercises.socraticHint: What does the protocol do when two machines answer the same question? Does it check anything before believing?

choices.text: ARP does not authenticate the answers: whoever answers is believed, and the answer sits in a cache for a few minutes.
choices.why: It is why HTTPS on a public network stops being a recommendation and becomes a necessity.

choices.text: ARP transmits the answers unencrypted, so they can be read and altered in transit.
choices.why: Reading is not the problem here: the attack works because the forged answer is accepted, not because the true one was read.

choices.text: The ARP cache never expires, so a forged answer is good for ever.
choices.why: The cache expires within minutes — the attacker has to repeat the answer, and that does not prevent the attack.

choices.text: ARP uses IP addresses instead of MAC ones, and so cannot tell machines on the same network apart.
choices.why: ARP does exactly the bridging between the two: it asks by IP and receives a MAC.

exercises.topic: Layered networks: from the cable to the browser
exercises.prompt: Put the layers in the order the data crosses them on the way **out** of your browser towards the network, from the highest to the lowest.
exercises.socraticHint: Each layer wraps the one above. Which of them produces the content all the others are going to wrap?
items: Application: the browser builds the HTTP request
Transport: the request is cut into segments and gets the ports
Network: each segment becomes a packet and gets the IP addresses
Link: each packet becomes a frame and gets the next hop's MAC
exercises.trap: The transport–network pair. Anyone who memorised "IP is the main one" tends to put the network layer before transport, as if the address came before the cutting into segments. It does not: transport is what decides the size of each piece and which program it belongs to, and only then does each piece get a destination address. Swapping the two would have the packet addressed before it exists.

exercises.topic: Layered networks: from the cable to the browser
exercises.prompt: A live video call uses UDP instead of TCP. What is the reasoning?
exercises.socraticHint: Ask what happens to a video frame that arrives half a second late. Is it still good for anything?

choices.text: In a live video, late data is already useless, and waiting for the resend would freeze the picture — better to lose the piece.
choices.why: The rule of thumb: if incomplete data is useless, TCP; if late data is useless, UDP.

choices.text: UDP encrypts the content by default, and video calls require confidentiality.
choices.why: UDP encrypts nothing; a call's encryption comes from another layer.

choices.text: TCP does not work with continuous data, only with files of known size.
choices.why: TCP carries a continuous stream without difficulty — it is what HTTP itself does.

choices.text: UDP guarantees faster delivery because it acknowledges each packet with fewer bytes.
choices.why: UDP acknowledges nothing: it is the absence of acknowledgement that makes it cheap.

exercises.topic: HTTP and HTTPS: methods, headers and status codes
exercises.prompt: An application deleted records through `GET /delete?id=7` links. After the site was indexed, several records vanished with nobody having clicked anything. What explains it?
exercises.socraticHint: Who besides a person follows the links on a page? And what promise does the `GET` method make to whoever follows them?

choices.text: `GET` promises to change nothing, so crawlers and prefetchers repeat it freely — and every visit carried out the deletion.
choices.why: The promise is not a formality: browsers, proxies and search engines rely on it.

choices.text: The search engine sent `DELETE` to the addresses it found, following the REST convention.
choices.why: Crawlers only issue `GET`; none of them sends `DELETE` on its own initiative.

choices.text: Indexing exposed the addresses, and people visited them manually.
choices.why: That may have happened too, but the cause that explains deletions with no click is the automatic repetition of the `GET`.

choices.text: The `200` returned by the deletion made the search engine repeat the request to confirm.
choices.why: A `200` does not ask for a repeat; the crawler repeats because `GET` is declared safe, whatever the status.

exercises.topic: HTTP and HTTPS: methods, headers and status codes
exercises.prompt: Match each status code to what it communicates. There are options left over in the right-hand column.
exercises.socraticHint: Two of them talk about identity and permission, and the difference between them is whether the server already knows who you are.

pairs.right: It has moved address for good
I do not know who you are
I know who you are, and you cannot
The server behind answered badly
You are asking too often

rightDistractors: The content has not changed since last time
The request is malformed and could not be interpreted

exercises.topic: HTTP and HTTPS: methods, headers and status codes
exercises.prompt: Tick everything TLS delivers on an HTTPS connection.
exercises.socraticHint: There are three guarantees, and one of them is what the padlock in the bar really stands for. Think too about what the network can still observe.

choices.text: Confidentiality: nobody along the path reads the content.
choices.why: It is the most remembered guarantee, and only one of the three.

choices.text: Integrity: altering the content in transit gives itself away.
choices.why: Without it, encrypting would not be enough — you could corrupt without reading.

choices.text: Authenticity: the certificate proves that server owns the domain.
choices.why: It is what the padlock stands for — "this really is the site whose name is in the bar", not "trustworthy site".

choices.text: Anonymity: the network cannot discover which domain was visited.
choices.why: The domain name and the volume of data stay visible to the network.

choices.text: Trustworthiness: the site was verified as reputable by an authority.
choices.why: The authority certifies ownership of the domain, not the honesty of whoever operates it.

exercises.topic: Cookies, sessions and browser cache
exercises.prompt: An application started running on two servers behind a load balancer. Users began getting "logged out" with no apparent pattern. What is the most likely cause?
exercises.socraticHint: The cookie carries only an identifier. Where is the data it identifies kept, and do both servers see the same place?

choices.text: The session is in each server's memory, so half the requests reach the one that does not have it.
choices.why: That is why a session in production lives somewhere shared — Redis, a database — or does not exist at all, and the state travels in a signed token.

choices.text: The cookie expires faster when more than one server is answering.
choices.why: The cookie's lifetime is declared in the `Set-Cookie` and does not depend on how many servers exist.

choices.text: The `SameSite` attribute blocks the cookie when the balancer switches servers.
choices.why: `SameSite` deals with requests coming from another site; the domain here is still the same.

choices.text: `HttpOnly` stops the second server from reading the cookie.
choices.why: `HttpOnly` stops the page's JavaScript from reading it; the server receives the cookie as normal.

exercises.topic: Cookies, sessions and browser cache
exercises.prompt: Match each directive or attribute to its effect. There are options left over in the right-hand column.
exercises.socraticHint: Three of them concern the cookie and one the cache. Two look like opposites and are not: one forbids keeping it, the other allows keeping it but demands confirmation.

pairs.right: The page's JavaScript cannot read the value
The value is not sent outside HTTPS
You may keep it, but confirm before reusing it
Do not keep it anywhere

rightDistractors: Reuse it without asking for the stated period
Encrypts the cookie value before writing it to disk

exercises.topic: Domains: registration, DNS, propagation and subdomains
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a server migration in order, so that no visitor lands on a dead address.
exercises.socraticHint: One of the steps has to happen well before the others for the rest to take effect quickly. Which of them depends on what the caches have already kept?
items: Lower the record's TTL to a few minutes, a day before the switch
Bring the application up on the new server and confirm it answers on its IP
Change the record to point at the new address
Confirm that the traffic is reaching the new server
Put the TTL back up to hours
exercises.trap: The lower-the-TTL–change-the-record pair. It is tempting to lower the TTL along with the change, or after it, to "speed up propagation". It does not work: the ceiling on the wait is the TTL that was already in force when the caches kept the old answer. Lowering it afterwards only affects the following queries, and the switch still takes the whole old TTL.

exercises.topic: Domains: registration, DNS, propagation and subdomains
exercises.prompt: You need to point `example.com`, without `www`, at a hosted service that only gives you a name (`app.provider.net`) and no IP. Why does a `CNAME` not solve it?
exercises.socraticHint: `CNAME` has a restriction on its position in the domain. Where exactly can it not exist, and which records already occupy that place?

choices.text: A `CNAME` cannot exist at the domain root, which has to coexist with other records such as the `MX`.
choices.why: The way out is `A` with fixed IPs, or an `ALIAS`/`ANAME`, a non-standard extension some providers offer.

choices.text: A `CNAME` only works for third-level subdomains or deeper.
choices.why: It works on any name that is not the root — `www.example.com` is second level and is accepted.

choices.text: A `CNAME` requires the target to be in the same domain as the name pointing at it.
choices.why: The target can be any name, including one belonging to another organisation.

choices.text: `CNAME` was deprecated in favour of `ALIAS` and is no longer honoured by resolvers.
choices.why: It is still in full use; it is `ALIAS` that is the non-standard extension.

exercises.topic: Hosting: shared, VPS, cloud and CDN
exercises.prompt: A shop with steady traffic all year round is migrating away from shared hosting. Tick the statements that hold up.
exercises.socraticHint: Two of the options sell elasticity to someone with no variation to stretch. And remember that the cost of a VPS is not only the invoice.

choices.text: A VPS transfers responsibility for updates, backups and the firewall to the shop.
choices.why: That is what really changes in the migration — not the power, but whose responsibility it is.

choices.text: The cloud's elasticity pays off little here, because there is no varying demand to follow.
choices.why: Elasticity pays off when demand varies; with steady traffic it usually costs more than a VPS.

choices.text: A CDN helps even without changing hosting, because it sits in front of it.
choices.why: The CDN does not replace the origin: it precedes it, and takes care of what is static.

choices.text: The cloud eliminates the noisy neighbour because resources are no longer shared.
choices.why: Shared instances still exist in the cloud; what changes is the isolation you pay for, not the absence of neighbours.

choices.text: Migrating to a VPS lowers the total cost, since the monthly invoice tends to be similar.
choices.why: The invoice is similar; the total cost rises in administration hours, which is where the sum really changes.

exercises.topic: Hosting: shared, VPS, cloud and CDN
exercises.prompt: After publishing a CSS fix, some visitors go on seeing the old version for hours. The site is behind a CDN. What is the structural solution?
exercises.socraticHint: There is the usual way out — asking the CDN to forget what it kept. And there is another, which makes the problem stop happening. What stops two different versions from competing for the same name?

choices.text: Give the file a name fingerprinted from its content, so that any change changes the name and the HTML points at a different address.
choices.why: It is the same solution as the cache lesson, now at world scale: different names never compete for the same cache.

choices.text: Reduce `max-age` to a few seconds on every static file.
choices.why: It works, but throws away the CDN's benefit — the file gets fetched again all the time.

choices.text: Turn the CDN off for the stylesheets and always serve them from the origin.
choices.why: It cures the symptom by giving up exactly the content that benefits most from the CDN.

choices.text: Send `no-store` on the HTML, which makes the CDN re-evaluate the files it references too.
choices.why: The directive applies to the document itself; it does not reach the files referenced by it.

exercises.topic: How the browser builds the page: DOM, CSSOM and rendering
exercises.prompt: Put the stages that lead from the HTML received to the pixels on screen in order.
exercises.socraticHint: Two trees are built before any position is computed. And position comes before colour.
items: The HTML is interpreted and becomes the DOM tree of objects
The CSS is interpreted and becomes the CSSOM
The final style of each node is computed, resolving inheritance and specificity
Layout computes the position and size of each box
Paint draws the pixels of each box
Composition puts the layers together on screen
exercises.trap: The layout–paint pair. Anyone thinking of "drawing the page" tends to merge the two into one step, or to swap them, imagining that the browser draws and then arranges. The separation is exactly what distinguishes a smooth animation from a stuttering one: changing `width` redoes the layout of everything around it, changing `background-color` only repaints, and changing `transform` touches only composition.

exercises.topic: How the browser builds the page: DOM, CSSOM and rendering
exercises.prompt: A sliding menu animation stutters on phones. It changes `left` on every frame. Which swap tends to fix it?
exercises.socraticHint: Each property triggers a different stage of rendering. Which of them does not force the browser to recompute where everything is?

choices.text: Animating `transform: translateX(...)`, which touches only composition and is handled by the graphics card.
choices.why: `transform` and `opacity` are the two properties that skip layout and paint.

choices.text: Animating `margin-left`, which is computed once and reused on the following frames.
choices.why: `margin-left` affects layout just as much as `left`, and is recomputed on every frame.

choices.text: Shortening the animation, since fewer frames mean less recomputation.
choices.why: Shortening it hides the symptom; the cost per frame stays the same.

choices.text: Moving the stylesheet to the end of the `<body>`, releasing rendering earlier.
choices.why: That changes when the page first appears, not the cost of each frame of the animation.

exercises.topic: Developer tools: network, console and elements
exercises.prompt: In the console of a page containing exactly three links (`<a>`), you type the two lines below. What appears?
exercises.socraticHint: The first line returns a collection of elements, and what is asked of it is a count. The second asks the type of the value.

exercises.topic: Developer tools: network, console and elements
exercises.prompt: In the Network tab, a request shows a high total time almost entirely spent waiting, with a fast transfer and a small size. What does that indicate?
exercises.socraticHint: The time splits between waiting for the response to start and receiving it. Which of the two speaks about the server and which about the path?

choices.text: The server took a long time to start answering — the bottleneck is the processing on the other side, not the connection.
choices.why: A fast transfer with a long wait isolates the problem in whoever answers.

choices.text: The user's connection is slow, which is why the total went up.
choices.why: A slow connection would show in the transfer, which here was fast.

choices.text: The response came from the cache, which explains the small size.
choices.why: A cached response is marked as such and does not sit waiting; the total time would be minimal.

choices.text: The file was compressed, and decompression consumed the waiting time.
choices.why: Decompression is local and fast; it does not show up as waiting for the server.

exercises.topic: ES6+ syntax: let/const, arrow functions and template strings
exercises.prompt: A variable declared with `const` is given an array. What is prevented from then on?
exercises.socraticHint: The restriction `const` imposes falls on the binding between the name and the value. Is the content that value points at subject to the same rule?

choices.text: Reassigning the variable to another value — but the array's contents can still be changed.
choices.why: `const` freezes the name↔value binding, not the object pointed at. `push` still works; `=` does not.

choices.text: Any change to the array, `push` and `pop` included, because `const` makes the value immutable.
choices.why: Immutable contents would require `Object.freeze`; `const` does not do that.

choices.text: Using the variable before the line it was declared on, which with `var` would be allowed.
choices.why: That is true of the temporal dead zone, and it applies equally to `let` — it is not what distinguishes `const`.

choices.text: Passing the variable as an argument to a function that changes the array it receives.
choices.why: Nothing stops it being passed, and the function can change the contents as normal.

exercises.topic: Types, coercion, strict equality and falsy values
exercises.prompt: In `0 == "0"` the result is `true`, but in `0 === "0"` it is `false`. What explains the difference?
exercises.socraticHint: One of the two operators has an extra step before comparing. What step would that be, and what does it do to the string?

choices.text: `==` converts the operands to a common type before comparing; `===` compares type and value without converting anything.
choices.why: It is the difference between abstract and strict equality: the first applies coercion, the second fails immediately when the types differ.

choices.text: `==` compares only the textual content of the values, ignoring whether they are a number or a string.
choices.why: There is no textual comparison: `0 == "0"` is true because the string becomes the number 0, not because `0` and `"0"` look alike written down.

choices.text: `===` only works between primitive values, so with a string it returns `false` because it cannot compare them.
choices.why: `===` works with any value, strings included; it returns `false` here because the types are different.

choices.text: `==` rounds numbers before comparing, and the rounding makes `0` coincide with the string.
choices.why: No rounding is involved: the conversion is from string to number, and `"0"` is already exactly 0.

exercises.topic: Types, coercion, strict equality and falsy values
exercises.prompt: Tick every value that is **falsy** in JavaScript — that is, that behaves like `false` inside an `if`.
exercises.socraticHint: The list of falsy values is closed and short. An empty object is still an object; an empty string is not the same thing as a string with one character in it.

choices.why: Zero is one of the values on the closed falsy list.

choices.text: `""` (the empty string)
choices.why: An empty string is falsy; any string with at least one character is truthy.

choices.text: `NaN`
choices.why: `NaN` is falsy, even though `typeof NaN` is `"number"`.

choices.text: `[]` (an empty array)
choices.why: Every object is truthy, and an array is an object — even an empty one. It is the classic trap: `[] == false` is `true`, but `if ([])` runs.

choices.text: `"0"` (a string with a zero)
choices.why: It is a one-character string, therefore truthy. Only the empty string is falsy.

exercises.topic: Types, coercion, strict equality and falsy values
exercises.prompt: Put the steps the interpreter takes when evaluating `"10" > 9` in order.
exercises.socraticHint: Before deciding how to compare, something has to be established about the operands. Comparing is the last thing that happens, not the first.
items: Establishes that the operands have different types: a string and a number
Converts the string `"10"` to the number 10, with ToNumber
Compares 10 with 9 numerically
Returns `true`
exercises.trap: The establish–convert pair. Anyone who learned that "the `>` operator converts the string" tends to put the conversion first, as if it were unconditional. It is not: with two strings (`"10" > "9"`) there is no conversion at all and the comparison is lexicographic, returning `false`. It is establishing the types that decides which of the two comparisons will happen, which is why it comes first.

exercises.topic: Selectors, cascade, inheritance and specificity
exercises.prompt: Two rules reach the same element: `#panel p { color: red }` and `.warning.featured p { color: blue }`. Which colour wins, and why?
exercises.socraticHint: Specificity is a trio compared from left to right. How many classes would it take to beat an id?

choices.text: Red: the id counts in the first number of the trio, and that is compared before the classes — no number of classes reaches it.
choices.why: (1,0,1) against (0,2,1): the first number decides and the others are never even consulted.

choices.text: Blue: two classes add up to more weight than one id, because the sum is a weighted total.
choices.why: The sum is not a total: it is a position-by-position comparison, and the first difference settles it.

choices.text: Blue: between rules reaching the same element, the one written last always wins.
choices.why: Order only breaks a tie when specificity ties, which is not the case here.

choices.text: Red: `color` is inherited, and inherited properties ignore specificity.
choices.why: Inheritance explains how a child gets a value with no rule of its own; here there are two direct rules, and the cascade decides.

exercises.topic: Box model, box-sizing and units (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)
exercises.prompt: An element has `width: 200px`, `padding: 20px` and `border: 2px`. How much horizontal space does it occupy, in CSS's default behaviour?
exercises.socraticHint: By default, `width` measures only one of the box's four layers. Which one — and do the others go inwards or outwards?

choices.text: 244px, because by default `width` measures only the content and padding and border add outwards.
choices.why: 200 + 20 + 20 + 2 + 2 = 244. It is what `box-sizing: border-box` corrects.

choices.text: 200px, because `width` always sets the element's final width on screen.
choices.why: That becomes true with `border-box`, which is not the default.

choices.text: 240px, because the border is drawn over the padding and adds no width.
choices.why: The border takes up space of its own, between padding and margin.

choices.text: 204px, because the padding is inside the content and does not add up.
choices.why: Padding is inside the box, but outside the content — and it adds up by default.

exercises.topic: Box model, box-sizing and units (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)
exercises.prompt: Tick the true statements about units.
exercises.socraticHint: One of them is the reason text sized in pixels is an accessibility problem. Another concerns a unit that compounds when elements nest.

choices.text: `rem` respects whoever enlarged the default font in the browser; `px` ignores that preference.
choices.why: It is why typography is measured in `rem`.

choices.text: `em` compounds in nested elements, because it is relative to the element's own font size.
choices.why: Two levels of `1.2em` give 1.44 times the size, not 1.2.

choices.text: On a phone, `svh` and `dvh` cope better than `vh` with the browser bar appearing and disappearing.
choices.why: `vh` pins the height to the larger window and leaves content hidden behind the bar.

choices.text: `%` is always relative to the size of the window.
choices.why: `%` is relative to the container; the ones referring to the window are `vw`/`vh`.

choices.text: `box-sizing: border-box` changes the meaning of `margin` as well as `width`.
choices.why: Margin is outside the box and is unaffected; what changes is what `width` and `height` measure.

exercises.topic: Flexbox: axes, alignment and distribution
exercises.prompt: In a container with `display: flex` and `flex-direction: column`, what does `justify-content: center` do?
exercises.socraticHint: The two alignment properties are not "horizontal" and "vertical": they are "main" and "cross". What has `flex-direction` just changed?

choices.text: It centres vertically, because with `column` the main axis has become the vertical one.
choices.why: `justify-content` always acts on the main axis, and it is `flex-direction` that decides which one that is.

choices.text: It centres horizontally, because `justify-content` always deals with the horizontal axis.
choices.why: It looks horizontal only because `row` is the default; with `column`, the one dealing with the horizontal is `align-items`.

choices.text: It does nothing, because in a column only `align-items` has any effect.
choices.why: Both go on working; what swapped was the axis each of them acts on.

choices.text: It centres in both directions, because `column` merges the axes.
choices.why: There are still two distinct axes; they merely changed orientation.

exercises.topic: Flexbox: axes, alignment and distribution
exercises.prompt: Match each declaration to the item's behaviour. There are options left over in the right-hand column.
exercises.socraticHint: Two of them differ only in the basis — `0` or `auto` — and it is the basis that decides whether the item's content influences the final width.

pairs.right: Stays at a fixed 240px, neither growing nor shrinking
Divides the space equally, ignoring the content
Takes whatever is left, starting from the content size
Allows shrinking below the content, avoiding the overflow

rightDistractors: Aligns the item on its own on the cross axis, ignoring its siblings
Changes the item's visual order without altering the HTML

exercises.topic: Responsiveness: mobile first, media queries and container queries
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of writing a responsive component mobile first in order.
exercises.socraticHint: One of the steps has no media query at all, and that is exactly why it comes first. Does measuring come before choosing where to break?
items: Write the one-column layout, with no media query at all
Widen the window until the one-column layout gets hard to read
Note that width down as the component's breakpoint
Add a `min-width` media query introducing the second column
exercises.trap: The measure–note pair. It is tempting to choose the breakpoint before looking, using the usual numbers (768, 1024). But a breakpoint is a property of the content, not of a device catalogue: the component breaks where reading gets worse, and that width changes with the text size and the density of each component. Fixing it before measuring produces a break in an arbitrary place and forces a correction later.

exercises.topic: Responsiveness: mobile first, media queries and container queries
exercises.prompt: A reusable card appears sometimes in a narrow bar and sometimes filling the whole screen. With a media query it comes out wrong in one of the two. Why?
exercises.socraticHint: A media query asks the size of what? And is that the measure determining the space the card actually received?

choices.text: The media query measures the window, not the space given to the card — and both cases happen in the same window.
choices.why: It is what container queries solve: `@container` measures the container, so the component adapts to the space it received.

choices.text: A media query is only re-evaluated on load, and not when the card moves.
choices.why: Media queries are re-evaluated continuously; the problem is what they measure, not when.

choices.text: `container-type` is missing from the card, so the media query does not take it into account.
choices.why: `container-type` enables `@container`, and does not change how `@media` behaves.

choices.text: The specificity of the rule inside the media query is lower than that of the base rule.
choices.why: A media query does not change specificity; the rule inside carries the weight of its own selector.

exercises.topic: Measures of central tendency: mean, median and mode
exercises.prompt: Write the expression for the variance of a sample `x` of `n` observations, about the mean `m`, using the denominator `n - 1`.
exercises.socraticHint: The numerator sums the squared deviations. The denominator is not `n` — ask yourself why the correction exists.

exercises.topic: Types, coercion, strict equality and falsy values
exercises.prompt: `[] == false` is `true` and `if ([])` runs the block. Both, at the same time. What explains it?
exercises.socraticHint: One of those two is a comparison and the other is a truthiness test. Are they the same operation?

choices.text: `==` converts both sides to numbers — `[]` becomes `0` and `false` becomes `0` — while `if` asks whether the value is truthy, and every object is truthy.
choices.why: Two different operations on the same value. `==` coerces; `if` consults the falsy list, which contains no object.

choices.text: `[]` is falsy, and `if ([])` running is a known engine bug kept for compatibility.
choices.why: `[]` is not falsy. The falsy list is closed: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`.

choices.text: `==` compares references and an empty array shares a reference with `false`.
choices.why: Nothing shares a reference with a primitive, and `==` between an object and a boolean does not compare references at all.

choices.text: `if` converts to string first, and the empty string is falsy.
choices.why: `if` converts to boolean, not to string — and `String([])` being `""` is a separate fact that does not apply here.

exercises.topic: Types, coercion, strict equality and falsy values
exercises.prompt: Which of these are falsy? Tick every one.
exercises.socraticHint: The list is closed and short. Anything not on it is truthy, however empty it looks.

choices.text: `NaN`
choices.why: On the list, despite `typeof NaN` being `"number"`.
The BigInt zero is on the list, like the Number zero.

choices.text: `document.all`
choices.why: It is falsy in browsers, and it is the one deliberate exception in the spec — not something to build on, and not what this asks about.

choices.text: `" "` (a single space)
choices.why: One character is one character. Only the EMPTY string is falsy.
An object, therefore truthy, however empty.

exercises.topic: ES6+ syntax: let/const, arrow functions and template strings
exercises.prompt: Reading a `let` before its declaration throws `ReferenceError`; reading a `var` gives `undefined`. What is the difference?
exercises.socraticHint: Both are hoisted. Ask what each is hoisted AS.

choices.text: `let` is hoisted but left uninitialised — the temporal dead zone — and reading an uninitialised binding throws. `var` is hoisted already initialised to `undefined`.
choices.why: Both bindings exist from the top of the scope. Only one of them has a value there.

choices.text: `let` is not hoisted at all, so the name does not exist until the line runs.
choices.why: If it did not exist, the lookup would reach an outer scope instead of throwing. It throws precisely because the inner binding is already there.

choices.text: `let` is block scoped and `var` is function scoped, and that is what produces the error.
choices.why: True and unrelated: the scoping difference explains WHERE the name is visible, not what reading it early does.

choices.text: `let` throws only in strict mode.
choices.why: The temporal dead zone is not a strict-mode behaviour; it applies everywhere `let` and `const` do.
