exercises.topic: Objects, arrays, spread and destructuring
exercises.prompt: In `const { a = 5 } = { a: null }`, what is `a`?
exercises.socraticHint: A default fires for exactly one absent value, and `null` is not it.

choices.text: `null` — a default fires only for `undefined`.
choices.why: Destructuring defaults test against `undefined` and nothing else. `null` is a value, so it is kept.

choices.text: `5` — the default fires for any empty value.
choices.why: "Empty" is not a thing the language tests for here; only `undefined` triggers a default.

choices.text: `undefined` — the default cancels the property.
choices.why: A default can only add a value, never remove one.

choices.text: A `TypeError`.
choices.why: Destructuring `null` from the right-hand side would throw; a property whose value is `null` does not.

exercises.topic: Types, coercion, strict equality and falsy values
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of `"5" - 2` in the order the engine performs them.
exercises.socraticHint: `-` has only one meaning, unlike `+`. That decides what it does with a string.
items: Sees `-`, which is defined for numbers alone
Converts `"5"` to the number 5, with ToNumber
Subtracts 2 from 5
Returns 3
exercises.trap: Anyone who learned this through `+` expects a string concatenation to be considered and rejected. It never is: `+` is overloaded and `-` is not, so there is no branch to take.

exercises.topic: Types, coercion, strict equality and falsy values
exercises.prompt: `NaN === NaN` is `false`. How do you test whether a value is `NaN`?
exercises.socraticHint: One of these answers is a function that first converts its argument.

choices.text: `Number.isNaN(v)`
choices.why: It tests the value as it is: `true` only for the actual `NaN`.

choices.text: `isNaN(v)`
choices.why: The global one coerces first, so `isNaN("abc")` is `true` — it answers "is not a number", which is a different question.

choices.text: `v === NaN`
choices.why: That is the comparison the question says does not work.

choices.text: `typeof v === "NaN"`
choices.why: `typeof NaN` is `"number"`.

exercises.topic: ES6+ syntax: let/const, arrow functions and template strings
exercises.prompt: Given `const list = [1, 2]`, which of these throw? Tick every one.
exercises.socraticHint: `const` freezes one thing, and it is not the contents.

choices.text: `list = [3]`
choices.why: Reassigning the binding is exactly what `const` forbids.

choices.text: `list = list`
choices.why: Still an assignment to the binding, whatever the right-hand side is.

choices.text: `list.push(3)`
choices.why: The contents are not frozen. `Object.freeze` would be needed for that.
Same reason: the binding is fixed, the object it points at is not.

exercises.topic: Selectors, cascade, inheritance and specificity
exercises.prompt: A `<span>` inside a styled `<div>` shows the div's `color` but not its `border`. Why?
exercises.socraticHint: Which of the two would be sensible to pass down to every descendant?

choices.text: `color` is an inherited property and `border` is not; inheritance is per-property and decided by the specification.
choices.why: Typography inherits, box decoration does not — otherwise every descendant would draw its own copy of the border.

choices.text: Borders need an explicit width, and the span has none.
choices.why: The div's border has a width; the question is why it is not passed down at all.

choices.text: A span is inline, and inline elements cannot have borders.
choices.why: They can. An inline border renders, it just does not affect line height.

choices.text: The span has higher specificity than the div.
choices.why: Specificity compares rules reaching the SAME element. Nothing here targets the span.

exercises.topic: Box model, box-sizing and units (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)
exercises.prompt: A box has `width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid`. With `box-sizing: border-box`, how wide does it render, and what does the content get?
exercises.socraticHint: The property renames what `width` measures. Ask which parts it now includes.

choices.text: 200px wide; the content gets 150px, because the padding and border are taken from the inside.
choices.why: `border-box` makes `width` the OUTER measurement, so everything else eats into it: 200 − 40 − 10 = 150.

choices.text: 250px wide; the content gets 200px.
choices.why: That is `content-box`, the default — where `width` measures the content and the rest is added on.

choices.text: 200px wide; the content gets 200px and the padding overflows.
choices.why: Padding does not overflow a box; it is part of it.

choices.text: 160px wide; the border is subtracted twice.
choices.why: The 5px is one border on each side, subtracted once as a total of 10.

exercises.topic: Flexbox: axes, alignment and distribution
exercises.prompt: With `flex-direction: column`, which property centres the children horizontally?
exercises.socraticHint: The two alignment properties are named after the axes, not after the screen.

choices.text: `align-items`, because with a column direction the horizontal axis is the CROSS axis.
choices.why: The direction swaps which axis is which; the property names follow the axis, not left-and-right.

choices.text: `justify-content`, which always handles the horizontal.
choices.why: It handles the MAIN axis, which in a column is vertical.

choices.text: `text-align: center` on the container.
choices.why: That centres inline content inside each child, not the children in the container.

choices.text: `margin: 0 auto` on the container.
choices.why: That centres the container in ITS parent, and says nothing about the children.

exercises.topic: Flexbox: axes, alignment and distribution
exercises.prompt: Three items in a row, each `flex: 1`. Which statements are true? Tick every one.
exercises.socraticHint: `flex: 1` is shorthand for three properties. One of them is not what people assume.

choices.text: They share the FREE space equally, not the total width.
choices.why: `flex-grow` distributes what is left over after the bases are laid out.

choices.text: `flex: 1` sets `flex-basis: 0`, which is why they usually end up equal anyway.
choices.why: With a basis of zero there is no leftover-versus-content distinction: all the width is free space.

choices.text: They will be equal even if one has much more text, with no other properties set.
choices.why: Because of the zero basis. This stops being true with `flex: auto`, whose basis is the content.

choices.text: `flex: 1` prevents them from shrinking below their content.
choices.why: Shrinking is `flex-shrink`, which `flex: 1` sets to 1. What resists shrinking is `min-width`, whose `auto` value is the usual culprit.

exercises.topic: Responsiveness: mobile first, media queries and container queries
exercises.prompt: Mobile first means writing the base styles for the small screen and adding `min-width` queries. What does that buy over the reverse?
exercises.socraticHint: Think about what a device that understands no media queries at all would render.

choices.text: The base stylesheet is the simplest layout, so anything that fails to apply a query still gets something usable.
choices.why: The fallback is the narrow layout, which works at any width. The reverse leaves a desktop layout on a phone.

choices.text: Media queries with `min-width` are faster to evaluate than `max-width`.
choices.why: There is no evaluation-cost difference; the argument is about what the base layer is.

choices.text: It is the only order in which media queries cascade correctly.
choices.why: Both orders cascade correctly. What differs is which layout is the default.

choices.text: It avoids needing `box-sizing: border-box`.
choices.why: Unrelated: `border-box` is worth setting either way.

exercises.topic: Responsiveness: mobile first, media queries and container queries
exercises.prompt: A card component must be narrow in a sidebar and wide in the main column, on the same page at the same viewport width. Media query or container query?
exercises.socraticHint: Ask what each one measures.

choices.text: Container query: it responds to the size of its own container, which is what differs here — the viewport is identical for both cards.
choices.why: A media query cannot tell the two cards apart, because there is nothing about the viewport that distinguishes them.

choices.text: Media query, with a breakpoint per placement.
choices.why: A breakpoint fires for the whole page. Both cards would get the same branch.

choices.text: Either; they measure the same thing with different syntax.
choices.why: One measures the viewport and the other the containing element. That is the whole distinction.

choices.text: Neither: this needs JavaScript.
choices.why: It did, before container queries. It does not now.

exercises.topic: Selectors, cascade, inheritance and specificity
exercises.prompt: Order the cascade's tests, from the one applied first to the one applied last.
exercises.socraticHint: Specificity is famous, and it is not the first thing consulted.
items: Origin and importance (author, user, user-agent; `!important` flips the order)
Specificity of the selector
Order of appearance — the later rule wins

exercises.topic: Box model, box-sizing and units (px, rem, em, %, vw/vh)
exercises.prompt: Two stacked block elements have `margin-bottom: 20px` and `margin-top: 30px`. How much space is between them?
exercises.socraticHint: Vertical margins between blocks do something horizontal ones never do.

choices.text: 30px — adjacent vertical margins collapse to the larger of the two.
choices.why: Margin collapsing takes the maximum, not the sum. It applies to vertical margins in normal flow.

choices.text: 50px — margins add up.
choices.why: They add up horizontally, and inside a flex or grid container. Between blocks in normal flow they collapse.

choices.text: 20px — the first element's margin wins because it comes first.
choices.why: Order does not decide it; size does.

choices.text: 0 — one of them is discarded.
choices.why: Collapsing merges them into one margin; it does not discard both.

rightDistractors: the request itself was malformed
moved for now — keep using this link

exercises.topic: HTTP and HTTPS: methods, headers and status codes
exercises.prompt: Which methods are idempotent — repeating the request leaves the server in the same state? Tick every one.
exercises.socraticHint: Idempotent is not the same as safe. One of these changes things and is still idempotent.

choices.text: `GET`
choices.why: Safe and therefore idempotent: it changes nothing at all.

choices.text: `PUT`
choices.why: It sets a resource to a given state. Doing it twice leaves the same state.

choices.text: `DELETE`
choices.why: The second delete finds nothing to delete; the end state is the same.

choices.text: `POST`
choices.why: The classic counter-example: two posts usually create two things, which is why double-submit is a real problem.

exercises.topic: Domains: registration, DNS, propagation and subdomains
exercises.prompt: Order the steps of resolving `www.example.com` from a cold cache.
exercises.socraticHint: The hierarchy is read right to left, and each step hands over a pointer rather than an answer.
items: The resolver asks a root server, which points at the `.com` servers
It asks a `.com` server, which points at example.com's nameservers
It asks example.com's nameserver, which answers with the address
The answer is cached for its TTL and returned to the browser
exercises.trap: Expecting the root server to know the address. It never does — every step above the last returns a referral, not a record.

exercises.topic: Domains: registration, DNS, propagation and subdomains
exercises.prompt: You are moving a site to a new host next week. What should you do to the DNS record's TTL, and when?
exercises.socraticHint: The TTL in force during the switch is the one that was published BEFORE it.

choices.text: Lower it well before the move, so the old value has already expired everywhere by the time you switch.
choices.why: Resolvers hold the value they last fetched. Lowering it at the moment of the switch changes nothing for anyone still holding the old one.

choices.text: Lower it at the moment of the switch — that is when the short TTL is needed.
choices.why: Too late: caches are already holding the old record for the old, long TTL.

choices.text: Raise it before the move, so fewer clients ask during the change.
choices.why: That makes the stale answer last longer, which is the opposite of what you want.

choices.text: Nothing; propagation is controlled by the registrar.
choices.why: The registrar delegates; the TTL on your record is what governs caching.

exercises.topic: Bandwidth, latency and throughput
exercises.prompt: A page of many small files loads slowly on a connection with plenty of bandwidth. Which number explains it?
exercises.socraticHint: One of these is measured in time and does not improve by widening the pipe.

choices.text: Latency: each file costs at least one round trip, and round trips do not get shorter with more bandwidth.
choices.why: Many small files is a latency-bound workload. Bandwidth helps a big file; it does not help waiting.

choices.text: Bandwidth: the files are competing for it.
choices.why: The premise says there is plenty of it.

choices.text: Throughput, which is a third quantity unrelated to the other two.
choices.why: Throughput is what you actually achieve — the symptom here, not the cause.

choices.text: Packet loss, which is the only thing that slows a fast link.
choices.why: Loss hurts, but a lossless high-latency link shows exactly this symptom.

exercises.topic: Cookies, sessions and browser cache
exercises.prompt: What does `SameSite=Lax` on a session cookie actually prevent?
exercises.socraticHint: It distinguishes requests by how they were STARTED, not by where they go.

choices.text: The cookie being sent on cross-site requests the user did not navigate with — a form post or an image load from another site.
choices.why: Top-level navigations still carry it, which is why following a link into the site keeps you signed in. That combination is what makes it a CSRF defence with usable ergonomics.

choices.text: The cookie being read by JavaScript on the page.
choices.why: That is `HttpOnly`.

choices.text: The cookie travelling over plain HTTP.
choices.why: That is `Secure`.

choices.text: Any request from a different origin, including a link the user clicked.
choices.why: That is `SameSite=Strict`, and it is why a link from an email logs you out on arrival.

exercises.topic: How the browser builds the page: DOM, CSSOM and rendering
exercises.prompt: Order the steps from receiving the HTML to pixels on screen.
exercises.socraticHint: Two trees are built before anything is positioned.
items: Parse the HTML into the DOM
Parse the CSS into the CSSOM
Combine them into the render tree
Lay out — compute the geometry of every box
Paint and composite
exercises.trap: Putting layout before the CSSOM. Geometry cannot be computed without the styles, which is why a stylesheet blocks rendering while a deferred script does not.

exercises.topic: IP address, MAC address and ARP
exercises.prompt: Your machine knows the destination's IP address. Why does it still need ARP?
exercises.socraticHint: The frame that leaves the network card is addressed to something else.

choices.text: To learn the MAC address for the next hop, because the link layer addresses frames by MAC and not by IP.
choices.why: IP identifies the endpoint; MAC identifies the machine on this segment. The frame needs the second.

choices.text: To check that the IP address is still assigned to somebody.
choices.why: That is not what ARP is for, even though a reply implies it.

choices.text: To find the shortest route to the destination network.
choices.why: That is routing, and it happens a layer up.

choices.text: To translate the domain name into the IP address.
choices.why: That is DNS, and the premise says the IP is already known.

exercises.topic: Layered networks: from the cable to the browser
exercises.prompt: Match each unit of data with the layer that produces it.
exercises.socraticHint: The names change as the data is wrapped on its way down.

pairs.right: link
network
transport
application

rightDistractors: physical
session

exercises.topic: Client, server and host: who asks and who answers
exercises.prompt: A machine runs a web server and also fetches an API from another machine. What is it?
exercises.socraticHint: The words describe a ROLE in one exchange, not a kind of computer.

choices.text: Both: server in one exchange and client in the other. The terms name a role per request, not a machine.
choices.why: This is the ordinary shape of every backend that calls another service.

choices.text: A server, because that is what it is configured as.
choices.why: Configuration does not fix the role of every exchange it takes part in.

choices.text: A host, which is a third category distinct from both.
choices.why: "Host" names the machine on the network; it is orthogonal to which role it plays.

choices.text: A proxy.
choices.why: A proxy forwards somebody else's request. Nothing here says it does.

exercises.topic: Measures of central tendency: mean, median and mode
exercises.prompt: Salaries at a small company: nine people earn 3,000 and the founder earns 300,000. Which measure describes what a typical person earns?
exercises.socraticHint: One of these is dragged by a single value and the other is not.

choices.text: The median, 3,000 — it is a position, so one extreme value moves it by at most one place.
choices.why: The mean here is 32,700, which nobody earns. That is what a skewed distribution does to a mean.

choices.text: The mean, because it uses every value and therefore describes the whole.
choices.why: It uses every value, which is exactly why one outlier drags it away from everybody.

choices.text: The mode, because it is the most common salary.
choices.why: It happens to equal the median here, but the mode says nothing about the rest of the distribution and does not exist for every dataset.

choices.text: Any of them; they agree on a dataset this small.
choices.why: They differ by an order of magnitude, which is the point of the example.

exercises.topic: Measures of central tendency: mean, median and mode
exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.socraticHint: Count the values before deciding which position is the middle.

exercises.topic: Measures of central tendency: mean, median and mode
exercises.prompt: Which statements about the mode are true? Tick every one.
exercises.socraticHint: Two of these are about existence and uniqueness rather than about value.

choices.text: A dataset can have more than one mode.
choices.why: Two values tied for most frequent gives a bimodal set.

choices.text: It is the only one of the three that works on categories, not just numbers.
choices.why: You cannot average colours; you can count which is most frequent.

choices.text: A dataset where every value appears once has no useful mode.
choices.why: Every value ties, so the mode says nothing.

choices.text: The mode is always one of the values in the dataset, and so is the median.
choices.why: The mode is; the median of an even-sized set is an average of two values and need not appear in it.

exercises.topic: Measures of central tendency: mean, median and mode
exercises.prompt: Order the steps of computing a median.
exercises.socraticHint: One step must happen before the position means anything.
items: Sort the values
Count them
If the count is odd, take the middle value
If it is even, average the two middle values
exercises.trap: Taking the middle of the list as written. The median is a position in the SORTED order, and skipping the sort gives an arbitrary element.

exercises.topic: Measures of central tendency: mean, median and mode
exercises.prompt: Adding one enormous value to a dataset. What happens to the mean and the median?
exercises.socraticHint: One is a computation over every value; the other is a position.

choices.text: The mean can move without bound; the median moves by at most one position in the sorted order.
choices.why: That bounded movement is what "robust to outliers" means, and it is why the median is preferred for skewed data.

choices.text: Both move without bound, since both use all the data.
choices.why: The median uses all the data to find a POSITION, and a single extra value shifts that position by one.

choices.text: Neither moves, since one value out of many is negligible.
choices.why: The mean moves by the value divided by the count, which is not negligible when the value is enormous.

choices.text: The median can move without bound and the mean is bounded.
choices.why: That is the two the wrong way round.

exercises.topic: Measures of central tendency: mean, median and mode
exercises.prompt: Match each measure with what it is.
exercises.socraticHint: One is a sum, one is a position, one is a count.

pairs.right: the sum divided by how many values there are
the value in the middle of the sorted order
the value that appears most often

rightDistractors: the difference between the largest and smallest
the average distance from the centre
